extracted.intended_audience: members of the Royal Society; mathematicians, natural philosophers, and astronomers (17th-century scientific readership)
extracted.subtask_description: Critically evaluating mathematical demonstrations, arithmetic computations, and astronomical observations in submitted papers — checking logical soundness, internal consistency, correct use of quantities/units, and adequacy of observational method and reporting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Logical soundness of demonstrations
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs and demonstrations must have valid logical grounds and not assert consequences without justification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page criticises Hobbes' demonstration as 'peccant' and notes there being 'no ground for such consequence.' An invalid proof that would 'serve as well for any proposition' (i.e., prove any proportion one pleases) is flagged as unacceptable. A demonstration must specifically establish the claimed relation rather than showing an indifferent / vacuous property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of proof to the claimed proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A demonstration should establish the particular proportion or equality asserted, not merely show an indifferent property that could apply to any proportion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author points out Hobbes' method 'proving indifferently every proportion' — such arguments are worthless because they do not actually prove the specific quadrature or equality claimed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internal consistency (no self-contradiction)
rubrics_metrics.description: The work must be internally consistent; definitions, propositions, and subsequent claims should not contradict one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes Hobbes' 'usual trade of contradicting himself' (e.g., first saying 'the side of a square is not a superficies, but a line' then the opposite). Contradictory statements across a work undermine credibility and must be avoided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correct use of dimensions / units (lengths vs areas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors must distinguish properly between quantities of different dimensions (e.g., lengths vs surfaces) and use units/terms accordingly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text corrects Hobbes: 'a bare number cannot be the side of a square' and insists that '10 lengths is the root of 100 squares.' Misstating lengths as areas (or vice versa) is a fundamental error; dimensional analysis must be respected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accurate arithmetic and fraction operations
rubrics_metrics.description: Computations, especially with fractions, must be performed correctly and reliably.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer accuses Hobbes of being 'miserably ignorant of the common operations of practical arithmetic,' giving examples where fractional multiplication and addition were mishandled, leading to incorrect numerical conclusions. Authors must reduce fractions and carry out multiplications precisely.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adherence to stated algorithms or rules
rubrics_metrics.description: When a method or 'rule' is given, the author must apply it correctly and consistently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer notes Hobbes' rule that 'the greatest root multiplied into itself' should be taken, yet Hobbes multiplies different quantities or misapplies his own rule. Follow-through on one's own procedure is required; exceptions must be justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Precision of definitions and terms
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions must be precise and used consistently; ambiguous or shifting meanings are unacceptable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: ambiguity about what is meant by 'greatest root' (sometimes 14+1/?, sometimes 14) creates confusion. Precise specification of what each term denotes (length, square, root, fraction) is necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agreement between geometric and arithmetic/calculus methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Different valid methods (geometrical constructions vs arithmetical calculations) applied to the same problem should yield consistent results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reviewer expects arithmetic computations and geometric (Euclidean) decompositions of areas to agree; discrepancies indicate errors in calculation or reasoning. Hobbes' conflicting 'arithmetical' and 'geometrical' results were due to mistakes rather than genuine method disagreement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper handling of infinities / suppositions of infinite processes
rubrics_metrics.description: When invoking infinite processes or 'supposed infinites,' authors should clarify whether they mean mathematical suppositions or claims about actual infinities and handle logical implications rigorously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text defends mathematicians' use of 'supposed infinites' but distinguishes between supposable infinite partitions and claims about actual infinite past durations. Arguments involving infinities must respect logical distinctions and geometric/logical requirements; crude or careless appeals to 'infinite' are insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rigour in claims of quadrature / mean-proportional constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that a straight line equals an arc or that a radius is a mean proportional between specified arcs must be backed by non-indifferent, specific demonstrations showing the equality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewer shows that Hobbes' repeated quadrature demonstrations could be made to 'prove' any claimed proportion; such constructions are invalid. A valid quadrature proof must not be indifferent to choice of parameters and must exclude trivial/general circularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate observational method and instrumentation (astronomy)
rubrics_metrics.description: Astronomical observations must use suitable instruments and techniques (e.g., telescopes, focal markers) to determine positions and motions accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signor Cassini used a three-foot glass, two fine threads crossing at right angles in the common focus to mark equator and declination circles; later observations used larger telescopes. Use of appropriate optics, alignment, and focal markers is required for reliable sunspot measurements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative reporting and reproducibility of observations
rubrics_metrics.description: Reports of observational phenomena should provide specific date/time stamps, angular sizes, positions relative to disk center, and measured motion so results are reproducible and period estimates can be derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The sunspot report gives dates (e.g., 11th–13th August 1671), positions ('about the third part of his semidiameter'), sizes ('one minute and 15 seconds' length, '30 seconds' breadth), and estimated diurnal motion (~13 degrees) and rotation period (~27.5 days). Such quantitative detail is the standard to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity of exposition: establish principles then derive consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Scholarly lectures/papers should first explain and establish underlying principles, then derive useful corollaries and applications, correcting common errors and filling defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The review of Barrow's Lectiones praises the structure: settling hypotheses, drawing general corollaries, prosecuting catoptrics and dioptrics, supplying demonstrations, and addressing errors. Good works state foundations clearly, proceed to derivations, and include demonstrations and corrective commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensiveness and practical applicability in scientific treatises
rubrics_metrics.description: A high-quality treatise should cover both theoretical result derivations and practical determinations (e.g., lens image positions), making it useful to practitioners as well as theorists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Barrow is commended for providing 'determinations of the places in the axis of the images' and for treating both points at infinite distance (parallel rays) and near points, thereby making theory serviceable to practice. Authors should include such practical guidance where relevant.
